tracks.title: Earth at night
tracks.subtitle: City lights, 2012 to 2023
tracks.description: One slow scan across the Earth at night for each year from 2012 to 2023. Bright cities ring notes; a deep hum follows all the light.

words.subject: planet
words.missing: not read. The far north and Antarctica are left out, because ice and snow there look like light.

tracks.summary: A slow scan line moves west to east across the Earth at night, once for each year from 2012 to 2023.

tracks.title: Night lights: what changed
tracks.subtitle: 2012 compared with 2023
tracks.description: NASA's map of how night lights changed from 2012 to 2023, scanned once, slowly. A rising pair of notes is new light; a low falling cello is light that dimmed.

words.map: map of change in night lights

tracks.summary: A slow scan line moves west to east once across NASA's map of how night lights changed from 2012 to 2023.

tracks.title: Air quality
tracks.subtitle: Four pollutants, summer 2024
tracks.description: NASA's model of the air we breathe in July and August 2024, a summer of huge wildfires. One scan for each pollutant: fine particles, carbon monoxide, nitrogen oxides and ozone. Clean air is a calm drone; dirty air rings notes and turns the drone sour.
tracks.units: position on NASA's colour scale for that pollutant

words.subject: planet
words.missing: not read. NASA's model has no reading here.

tracks.title: Ocean currents
tracks.subtitle: Surface currents, 2007 to 2008
tracks.description: Starts with a guided lesson: what a current is, then the Gulf Stream's direction, speed and changes, one idea at a time. Then a scan line crosses NASA's world map of the ocean's surface currents, March 2007 to March 2008: only what is under the line plays.

words.subject: ocean
words.missing: land, or too far north, so there is no current reading here. Try a place at sea.

tracks.title: Carbon dioxide
tracks.subtitle: Seven weeks of early 2020
tracks.description: NASA's model of carbon dioxide from 14 January to 3 March 2020, flattened from its turning globe into one world map. A scan line crosses it west to east: dense carbon dioxide rings a note, and a deep hum follows everything under the line.
tracks.units: share of the densest carbon dioxide

words.subject: planet
words.missing: too far north or south for NASA's turning globe, so there is no reading here.

tracks.title: Lightning
tracks.subtitle: 2017 to 2023, in 14 parts
tracks.description: Lightning seen from the International Space Station, March 2017 to July 2023, in 14 parts, in order. Each stormy place plays a drop-like note; listen to the storms swing north and south with the seasons.

words.subject: planet
words.missing: outside what the space station can see. Its sensor covers only about 55 degrees north to 55 degrees south.

tracks.title: Atmospheric river
tracks.subtitle: A river in the sky, December 2010
tracks.description: NASA's 3D film of an atmospheric river: a long, narrow band of water vapour flowing from near Hawaii to the mountains of California in December 2010. The hum is the vapour in the picture, a kalimba note falls where the river's core crosses, and a soft pulse marks each midnight on NASA's clock, which is shown over the film.
tracks.units: water vapour in the picture, relative

words.subject: atmosphere
words.missing: not a place on a map. This track follows NASA's moving camera, so it has no map of places to explore. Try Air quality or Earth at night.

tracks.title: El Niño: then and now
tracks.subtitle: Sea temperature, 2025 and 2026
tracks.description: NASA's map of how much warmer or cooler than normal the sea is, one map a month: each month of 2025, then the same month of 2026. A rising pair of notes is sea much warmer than normal; a low falling cello, much cooler. Listen to the middle of the Pacific: in 2026, El Niño warms it.
